edges.description: Infection-associated immune activation may generate cross-reactive antiviral immune responses.
Infection-associated CNS injury may expose normally sequestered CNS antigens to the immune system.
Putative pathogen-cross-reactive lymphocytes may initiate CNS-directed inflammation, but this route has not been demonstrated in most patients.
CNS antigen release and tolerance breakdown may generate autoreactive immune responses, but the route is based mainly on mechanistic models.
CNS-directed inflammation converges on the characteristic perivenous demyelinating lesion pattern.
intermediate_mechanisms: inflammatory cells and soluble mediators concentrated around CNS venules

edges.description: Multifocal CNS inflammation can disrupt arousal networks and produce reduced consciousness; lesion location and edema likely mediate the link.
The multifocal inflammatory lesion distribution can extend into the thalami.
The multifocal inflammatory lesion distribution can extend into the basal ganglia.
CNS-directed inflammation produces the characteristic large, poorly demarcated white-matter lesion pattern through incompletely resolved cellular injury pathways.
Extension of multifocal CNS inflammation to the spinal cord produces the myelitis component of some attacks.
Extension of inflammatory demyelination to the optic nerve can produce optic neuritis during the index attack.
Cerebellar, brainstem, or connected-tract inflammation can manifest as ataxia.
Cortical or network-level inflammatory dysfunction can lower seizure threshold during the acute attack.
Fever can accompany the acute inflammatory syndrome, although infection and other mimics must be excluded and the causal source may be systemic.
Meningeal irritation, cytokine signaling, or raised intracranial pressure may mediate headache during acute CNS inflammation.
Inflammation affecting corticospinal tracts, brainstem, or spinal cord can produce pyramidal motor weakness.
CNS immune-cell recruitment can be reflected by a mild, variable increase in CSF leukocytes.
Acute inflammatory injury and network disruption may leave persistent cognitive or academic sequelae even after motor recovery.
Perivenous loss of CNS myelin is the tissue lesion represented by the clinical and MRI demyelination phenotype.
Multifocal inflammatory lesions and associated cortical network dysfunction are associated with the obligatory encephalopathy phenotype, although the exact route is unresolved.

Most events follow a respiratory or gastrointestinal illness by days to weeks. Recorded as direct because this node is the antecedent itself rather than a downstream consequence of it; what the antecedent then does is modelled by the mimicry and barrier nodes further along.

Reported after immunisation but not established as a general cause, and the cited source argues against reading it as one. Graded well below the preceding-infection link into this same node, and worded so that adding the link does not quietly convert a contested temporal report into a mechanism.

nodes.description: The classic microscopic lesion pattern in ADEM is perivenous inflammatory demyelination, with macrophage, lymphocyte, and microglial inflammatory cells surrounding small veins and clearing myelin. This pattern helps distinguish ADEM from typical confluent multiple-sclerosis plaques, although mixed or overlapping pathology can occur.
